title: Positive Definite Binary Quadratic Forms and Reduction

items.title: Integral binary quadratic forms
Integers represented, and primitively represented, by a binary quadratic form
Primitive binary quadratic forms
The discriminant of a binary quadratic form
An integer is the discriminant of an integral binary quadratic form exactly when it is congruent to $0$ or $1$ modulo $4$
items.strategy: Necessity is the square-class check modulo $4$. Sufficiency uses the explicit forms $(1,0,-\Delta/4)$ and $(1,1,(1-\Delta)/4)$, matching the two congruence classes.

items.title: The principal binary quadratic form of a discriminant
Proper equivalence of binary quadratic forms
Integral substitution defines a right action of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ on integral binary quadratic forms
items.strategy: Write $f\mid M$ for substitution by the integer matrix $M$. The identity matrix fixes every form, and associativity of matrix multiplication gives $(f\mid M)\mid N=f\mid(MN)$.

items.title: Properly equivalent binary quadratic forms represent the same integers, with primitive representations in bijection
items.strategy: If $g=f\mid M$ and $g(x,y)=n$, then $f(M(x,y))=n$. The inverse matrix of $M=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ is explicit because $ps-qr=1$, so the same argument runs backwards. Primitive vectors stay primitive under unimodular substitution by the Bézout-style formulas for the inverse coordinates.

items.title: Proper equivalence preserves discriminant and primitivity of the form
items.strategy: Compute the transformed coefficients under a general determinant-one substitution. The discriminant changes by the square of the determinant, and the new coefficients generate the same ideal in $\mathbb Z$ as the old ones because the inverse substitution is again integral.

items.title: Some discriminant $\Delta$ form primitively represents $n$ exactly when $\Delta$ is a square modulo $4n$
items.strategy: From a primitive representation $n=f(r,s)$, extend $(r,s)$ to a determinant-one matrix and move the represented integer into the leading coefficient, so the discriminant becomes a square modulo $4n$. Conversely, if $b^2\equiv\Delta\pmod{4n}$, the form $nx^2+bxy+cy^2$ with $c=(b^2-\Delta)/(4n)$ has discriminant $\Delta$ and primitively represents $n$ at $(1,0)$.

items.title: Positive-definite binary quadratic forms
An integral binary quadratic form is positive definite exactly when its leading coefficient is positive and its discriminant is negative
items.strategy: Complete the square in $4af(x,y)=(2ax+by)^2-\Delta y^2$. This gives one direction immediately and the converse by checking positivity on all nonzero real pairs.

items.title: Reduced positive-definite binary quadratic forms
A non-reduced positive-definite form admits an equivalent positive-definite form with smaller reduction measure
items.strategy: Use the two Gauss moves: swap $(a,b,c)\mapsto(c,-b,a)$ when $c<a$, and shear $(a,b,c)\mapsto(a,b+2ka,ak^2+bk+c)$ with $b+2ka\in(-a,a]$ when $|b|>a$. Except for the final boundary normalization $a=c$ and $b<0$, one of these moves strictly improves the integer measure $a+|b|$.

items.title: Every positive-definite integral binary quadratic form is properly equivalent to a reduced form
items.strategy: Iterate the Gauss moves until the reduction measure cannot decrease further, then do the single boundary sign flip when $a=c$ and $b<0$. The measure is a positive integer, so the algorithm terminates.

items.title: The leading coefficient of a reduced positive-definite form is minimal in its proper-equivalence class
items.strategy: If $g=f\mid\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, then the new leading coefficient is $f(p,r)$. Because $(p,r)$ is primitive, the reduced-form inequalities force $f(p,r)\ge a$.

items.title: Properly equivalent reduced forms with the same leading coefficient are equal
items.strategy: Equality of the leading coefficient forces the transformation matrix to have first column $(1,0)$ or $(-1,0)$; the reduced-form interval $(-a,a]$ for the middle coefficient and the boundary sign convention then force the shear parameter to vanish, so the coefficients agree term by term.

items.title: Each proper-equivalence class of positive-definite integral binary quadratic forms contains exactly one reduced form
items.strategy: Existence is the reduction theorem. If two reduced forms are properly equivalent, the minimal-leading-coefficient lemma gives equality of their leading coefficients, and the same-leading-coefficient lemma then forces equality of the whole triples.

items.title: A reduced positive-definite form of discriminant $\Delta$ satisfies $a\le\sqrt{|\Delta|/3}$
items.strategy: For a reduced form, $b^2\le a^2\le ac$. Substituting into $|\Delta|=4ac-b^2$ gives $|\Delta|\ge 3a^2$, which is the required bound.

items.title: For each negative discriminant, there are only finitely many proper-equivalence classes of positive-definite integral binary quadratic forms
items.strategy: Every class has one reduced representative, and the reduced inequalities together with the leading-coefficient bound leave only finitely many triples $(a,b,c)$.

items.title: The class number of primitive positive-definite binary quadratic forms of discriminant $\Delta$
Proper equivalence of positive-definite integral binary quadratic forms is decidable
items.strategy: Reduce both forms and compare the unique reduced representatives. Equality of the reduced triples is equivalent to proper equivalence.

title: Positive Definite Binary Quadratic Forms and Reduction — Examples

items.title: Reducing $(458,214,25)$ to $(1,0,1)$
items.strategy: Run the explicit swap-and-shear algorithm, record the intermediate forms, and multiply the corresponding matrices to one determinant-one matrix carrying the original form to $x^2+y^2$.

items.title: The reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-4$
items.strategy: Use the bound on the leading coefficient to force $a=1$, then solve the discriminant equation under the reduced inequalities. Conclude that $(1,0,1)$ is the unique reduced primitive form and that $h(-4)=1$.

items.title: The reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-8$
items.strategy: Enumerate the reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-8$ exactly as for $-4$. The only possibility is $(1,0,2)$, so the unique reduced primitive form is $x^2+2y^2$ and $h(-8)=1$.

items.title: Odd primes congruent to $1$ or $3$ modulo $8$ are represented by $x^2+2y^2$
items.strategy: Show directly that any value of $x^2+2y^2$ at an odd prime is $1$ or $3$ modulo $8$. For the converse, combine the two reciprocity supplements to get $(-2/p)=1$, turn a solution of $t^2\equiv-2\pmod p$ into the discriminant-square condition for $\Delta=-8$, invoke the primitive-representation criterion, and then use the unique reduced form of discriminant $-8$.

items.title: The reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-20$
items.strategy: Enumerate the reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-20$ under the same bound. The two reduced primitive forms give the form class number $h(-20)=2$.

items.title: The reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-23$
items.strategy: Enumerate the reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-23$ and check that the two signs of the middle coefficient can survive as distinct reduced forms. This produces the three reduced primitive classes and $h(-23)=3$.

items.title: Forms of discriminant $-24$ need not be properly equivalent
items.strategy: Compare $(1,0,6)$ and $(2,0,3)$. They share discriminant $-24$, but the first represents $1$ and the second does not, so representation preservation rules out proper equivalence.

items.title: Distinct reduced forms can represent the same integers
items.strategy: Use $(2,1,3)$ and $(2,-1,3)$. Check that each reduced form represents exactly the same integers by the substitution $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, but the uniqueness theorem forbids proper equivalence because the reduced triples are distinct.

items.title: Improper equivalence can merge two distinct proper classes
items.strategy: The determinant $-1$ substitution $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$ carries $(2,1,3)$ to $(2,-1,3)$. This shows exactly what forgetting orientation changes: the two forms are improperly equivalent although the reduced-form uniqueness theorem shows they are not properly equivalent.

items.title: An indefinite proper-equivalence class can contain a cycle of reduced forms
items.strategy: Write out Granville's positive-discriminant reduced-form convention and verify two distinct reduced forms in his discriminant-$60$ cycle. This separates the positive-definite uniqueness theorem from the indefinite reduction theory that belongs with Pell equations and continued fractions.
